I’ve been farming these 70 mu for six years now, so I know what my family of three can handle. With only the three of us, I have to be careful with labor, but I’ve got a reliable well, so water isn’t the main worry—electricity bills are. I’ve learned that the wheat-maize double crop is my safety net: the price is steady, the machines do most of the work, and the buyers come right to the field. So I’ll keep 40 mu in that rotation. I buy improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed from the dealer in town because the yield jump over traditional seed is obvious; after six seasons I don’t even think about going back. For the other 30 mu I need cash crops that pay the bigger bills. Watermelon and chili sell well at the wholesale market in Handan, but they’re hand-labor crops, so I’ll limit them to 8 mu and 6 mu. Cotton is still decent money around here and not as frantic as vegetables, so I’ll plant 12 mu. I always plough cotton deep so the roots can go down, but for the rest I use rotary tillage to save time and diesel. I’ll put 4 mu into autumn cauliflower because that fills the gap after the summer rush and the cooler weather means fewer pest headaches. On fertilizer, I follow what the ag-tech station in Quzhou recommends: roughly 15–18 kg of nitrogen per mu for grains, a bit less phosphorus, and potassium where the soil tests low. I spray pesticides only when I see damage—except cotton and vegetables, where I stay ahead of the bollworm and aphids with a few extra applications. Irrigation will be 3–6 times depending on the crop, pumped straight from the well.
